title: What do the NDIS restrictive practices rules require of implementing providers and behavior support practitioners?
description: NDIS Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support Rules 2018: five regulated practices, plan deadlines, monthly reports, records and practitioner suitability.
shortAnswer: The NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018 make five regulated restrictive practices lawful in NDIS supports only under conditions. Implementing providers must be registered, obtain state or territory authorization, follow the behavior support plan, report use to the NDIS Commission monthly and keep detailed records for seven years. Plans containing these practices must be written by an NDIS behavior support practitioner the Commission has found suitable, and reviewed at least every 12 months.
keyTakeaways: The five regulated restrictive practices are seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint and environmental restraint (section 6).
Where a practice will continue without a plan, the implementing provider must take all reasonable steps to have an interim plan within 1 month and a comprehensive plan within 6 months of first use.

Implementing providers report use monthly (within 5 business days of month end, per the Commission), or every 2 weeks under a short term state approval, and keep eight categories of record for seven years.
Practitioners are assessed against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework; updated assessment processes apply to new applicants from December 18, 2026.
Module 2A of the Practice Standards expects workers to be trained in the safe use of restrictive practices and supported to implement each plan's strategies.
regulator: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, with state and territory authorization bodies for restrictive practice approvals
appliesTo: Registered NDIS providers that implement behavior support plans or use regulated restrictive practices (implementing providers)
Specialist behavior support providers registered for group 0110
NDIS behavior support practitioners and applicants for suitability
Support workers, team leaders and key personnel of implementing providers

sections.heading: What do the NDIS Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support Rules cover?

blocks.text: The rules set conditions of registration for two groups: providers who use regulated restrictive practices, and specialist behavior support providers who write the plans. They are the [National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2018L00632/latest/text) (the Behaviour Support Rules), made under section 73H of the NDIS Act; the current compilation on the Federal Register of Legislation is dated December 1, 2020. This page states the position as at November 2026.

Section 6 limits the rules to five regulated restrictive practices: **seclusion** (sole confinement where voluntary exit is prevented, not facilitated or implied not to be permitted), **chemical restraint** (medication used primarily to influence behavior, excluding medication prescribed to treat a diagnosed mental disorder, physical illness or condition), **mechanical restraint** (a device used primarily to influence behavior), **physical restraint** (physical force used primarily to influence behavior, excluding a reflexive hands on technique to guide a person away from harm) and **environmental restraint** (restricting free access to parts of the environment, items or activities).

Breach of these conditions can attract a civil penalty, because the rules note that section 73J of the Act applies to breaches of registration conditions. The NDIS Commission states that it is a breach of the NDIS rules for an unregistered provider to use regulated restrictive practices at all ([rules for implementing providers](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers)). A broader view of NDIS training obligations is in [what training NDIS workers need](/regulations/ndis-practice-standards-worker-training).

sections.heading: What must an implementing provider do before and after using a restrictive practice?

blocks.text: An implementing provider must be registered, be audited against Module 2A of the Practice Standards, obtain authorization where the state or territory requires it, use the practice only as the plan says, and report and record each use. The NDIS Commission notes that the term implementing provider is not defined in legislation; it covers any NDIS provider that implements behavior support plans or uses regulated restrictive practices in delivering supports.

items: **Respect prohibitions (section 8).** If a state or territory prohibits a practice, the provider must not use it.

**Obtain authorization (section 9).** Any use other than a single emergency use must be authorized under the state or territory process, and evidence must be lodged with the Commissioner as soon as reasonably practicable.

**Follow the plan (section 10).** A regulated restrictive practice in a plan must be used only in accordance with the plan, and the provider must tell the specialist behavior support provider about a change in circumstances that requires review.

**Facilitate a plan where none exists (sections 11 to 13).** If use is likely to continue, the provider must take all reasonable steps to have an interim plan developed within 1 month, and a comprehensive plan within 6 months, after the first use. Where the use was unauthorized, it must also seek authorization as soon as reasonably practicable.

**Report (section 14).** Monthly reports to the Commissioner on use of regulated restrictive practices, or every 2 weeks while a short term state or territory approval is in force. The Commission asks for monthly reports within 5 business days of month end, including months when a practice was not used.
**Record (section 15).** Written records of each use, kept for seven years from the day the record is made.

blocks.text: Unauthorized use is also a reportable incident. The Commission defines a practice as unauthorized if it is not in a plan, not authorized under the state or territory process, or not used as the plan specifies, and requires it to be notified within 5 business days of the provider becoming aware ([rules for implementing providers](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers)). The notification process is covered in [NDIS incident management and reportable incidents](/regulations/ndis-incident-management-and-reportable-incidents-training).

sections.heading: What must be recorded each time a regulated restrictive practice is used?

blocks.text: Section 15(2) of the Behaviour Support Rules lists the minimum content, and every item depends on the worker who was present. That makes record writing a trained skill, not an administrative afterthought.

items: A description of the use, including its impact on and any injury to the person or others, whether it was a reportable incident, and why it was used.
The behavior that led to the use.
The time, date and place the use started and ended.
Names and contact details of the persons involved and of any witnesses.
Actions taken in response to the use.
Less restrictive options considered or used first.
Actions taken leading up to the use, including strategies used to prevent the need for it.

blocks.text: The last two items test whether workers know and apply the proactive strategies in the plan. A record that says only that a restraint was applied for a stated time cannot show that less restrictive options were tried.

sections.heading: What must behavior support practitioners and specialist providers do?

blocks.text: Specialist behavior support services must be delivered by an NDIS behavior support practitioner (section 17), and only a practitioner may develop a plan containing a regulated restrictive practice (section 18). The NDIS Commission states that until it considers a person suitable, they cannot undertake behavior support assessments or develop plans, even under supervision ([apply to become a practitioner](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/apply-become-ndis-behaviour-support)).

items: **Timeframes (section 19):** an interim plan within 1 month, and a comprehensive plan within 6 months, after being engaged to develop it. The Commission treats the provider as engaged from the service agreement date or a start date specified in it.

**Development (section 20):** take all reasonable steps to reduce and eliminate the need for regulated restrictive practices, consult the person, their family, carers or guardian and the implementing provider, give details of the intended practice in an accessible format, and complete a functional behavioural assessment for a comprehensive plan.

**Content (section 21):** evidence based, person centred, proactive strategies, and any practice must be clearly identified, authorized where required, a last resort, the least restrictive response, proportionate and used for the shortest possible time.
**Review (section 22):** a comprehensive plan must be reviewed when circumstances change and at least every 12 months.
**Lodgment (section 24):** every plan containing a regulated restrictive practice must be lodged with the Commissioner as soon as practicable, whether or not state authorization is required.

blocks.text: Specialist behavior support providers must be registered with group 0110 Specialist positive behaviour support ([rules for practitioners](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-behaviour-support-and)). Since October 12, 2026, new plans are lodged in the new NDIS Commission Portal; the Commission states that draft plans left in the existing portal on that date were removed and cannot be recovered.

sections.heading: How is practitioner suitability assessed, and what changes in December 2026?

blocks.text: Suitability is assessed against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, which has four capability levels: core, proficient, advanced and specialist. The Commission decides only 'suitable', 'not suitable' or 'unable to make a decision'; it does not endorse a capability level ([Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/positive-behaviour-support)).

There are two pathways. The self-assessment pathway uses a self-assessment against the framework and a supervisor endorsed portfolio. The new entry-level pathway is for applicants with less than 6 months positive behavior support experience or a limited portfolio; they must be supervised by a practitioner at proficient level or above, with a professional development plan and supervisor agreement. The Commission may find a new entry-level applicant not suitable to operate as a sole trader or key personnel of a specialist provider unless they will employ a proficient practitioner with 2 years' experience, and it aims to process most applications within 4 to 6 weeks.

blocks.title: In transition: updated assessment from December 18, 2026
blocks.text: The NDIS Commission has completed a review of the framework and states that, from December 18, 2026, updated assessment processes aligned to the updated framework will apply to new applicants seeking suitability. Practitioner development plans written now should be checked against the updated framework and resources.

sections.heading: What training do Module 2A and the rules expect for support workers?

blocks.text: The Behaviour Support Rules do not set a course or hours for support workers; the training expectations come from the quality indicators in Module 2A of the Practice Standards, against which implementing providers are audited ([Module 2A](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/ndis-practice-standards/supplementary-module-implementing-behaviour-support)). Several indicators go beyond the general access to training already covered on the [NDIS worker training page](/regulations/ndis-practice-standards-worker-training).

items: Workers receive training in the safe use of restrictive practices.
Workers maintain the skills required to use restrictive practices and help the participant and others understand the associated risks.
Specialist behavior support providers are supported to train the implementing provider's workers in the use and monitoring of the plan's strategies.
Workers are supported and facilitated to receive training in implementing an interim behavior support plan.
After an unauthorized use, workers and management debrief to identify improvements, and the outcomes are documented.
Performance management checks that workers are implementing plan strategies appropriately, and monthly reporting data is fed back to workers.

blocks.text: The Commission also describes shared responsibility: specialist and implementing providers working together to give NDIS workers person focused training so they can implement each plan effectively. In practice that means plan specific training for the named participant, not a generic course alone.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each section of the Behaviour Support Rules and each Module 2A indicator as an obligation linked to the concepts a worker must understand, such as the five practice definitions and the section 15 record fields, and to an assessment point. Plan specific training can then be traced to a named participant and plan version, which is the evidence an auditor asks for.

faqs.q: Is a single emergency use of a restrictive practice a breach?
faqs.a: Section 9 exempts a single emergency use from the prior authorization requirement, but the use still has to be recorded under section 15, and if it was not authorized or not in a plan it is a reportable incident that must be notified to the NDIS Commission within 5 business days. If use is likely to continue, plan and authorization duties start.

faqs.q: Can an unregistered provider implement a behavior support plan with a restrictive practice?
faqs.a: No. The NDIS Commission states that providers implementing plans containing regulated restrictive practices must be registered and audited against Module 2A, and that it is a breach of the NDIS rules for an unregistered provider to use regulated restrictive practices. Plans for participants supported by unregistered providers can note this when lodged.

faqs.q: How long must restrictive practice records be kept?
faqs.a: Seven years from the day each record is made, under section 15(3) of the Behaviour Support Rules. The record must include the behavior that led to the use, start and end times, people and witnesses involved, less restrictive options considered, and actions taken before and after.

faqs.q: Do support workers need a specific qualification to implement restrictive practices?
faqs.a: The rules do not prescribe one. Module 2A expects workers to receive training in the safe use of restrictive practices, to maintain the skills required, and to be supported to implement each participant's plan strategies, with performance management checking that they do. Providers should evidence competence for each plan, not only course completion.

factCheck.claim: Behaviour Support Rules s 6 defines the five regulated restrictive practices: seclusion, chemical, mechanical, physical and environmental restraint, with stated exclusions; latest compilation dated 1 December 2020; Parts 2 and 3 made under s 73H with note on s 73J civil penalty.

Behaviour Support Rules ss 8 to 13: prohibition, authorisation other than single emergency use with evidence lodged as soon as reasonably practicable, use only per plan and notify specialist of changes, facilitate interim plan within 1 month and comprehensive plan within 6 months after first use.
Behaviour Support Rules s 14 monthly reports, or every 2 weeks under short term approval; s 15 record contents and 7 year retention.

Behaviour Support Rules ss 17 to 24: practitioner requirement, interim plan 1 month and comprehensive 6 months after engagement, development steps including functional behavioural assessment, content requirements, review at least every 12 months, lodgement regardless of authorisation.

Implementing provider not defined in legislation; must be registered and audited against Module 2A; unregistered use is a breach; monthly reporting within 5 business days of month end including when not used; unauthorised restrictive practice reportable within 5 business days.

Specialist providers need registration group 0110; engagement date is service agreement date or specified date; from 12 October 2026 plans lodged in new portal and drafts left in old portal were removed.

Cannot undertake assessments or plans before suitability even under supervision; two pathways; new entry-level under 6 months experience, proficient supervisor; sole trader limits with 2 years experience; 4 to 6 weeks processing.

Framework has four levels core, proficient, advanced, specialist; Commission decides suitable, not suitable or unable to decide; updated assessment processes apply to new applicants from 18 December 2026.

Module 2A indicators: workers receive training in safe use of restrictive practices; maintain skills; specialist providers supported to train workers; interim plan training; documented debriefing after unauthorised use; performance management.
